Physiology-01.question: ১) Average value of MCH
Physiology-01.exp:
MCH (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin) is the average amount of hemoglobin present in a single red blood cell.

  • Normal MCH value: ≈ 27–32 pg

  • Average value: ≈ 29 pg 

Other RBC indices:

  • MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume) → Normal ≈ 90 fL

  • MCHC (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration) → Normal ≈ 33–36 g/dL

  • Hematocrit (PCV) → Normal ≈ 45%

Exam pearl:

  • MCV → 90 fL (size of RBC)

  • MCH → 29 pg (Hb amount per RBC)

  • MCHC → 33 g/dL (Hb concentration in RBC)

Physiology-01.question: ২) Which is substrate for Lysosomal enzyme cathepsins?
Physiology-01.exp:
Cathepsins are lysosomal proteolytic enzymes that digest proteins into smaller peptides and amino acids.

  • Cathepsins are mainly cysteine proteases present inside lysosomes.

  • They play an important role in intracellular protein degradation and autophagy.

Exam pearl:
Lysosomal enzymes:

  • Cathepsins → Protein digestion

  • DNase → DNA degradation

  • RNase → RNA degradation

  • Lipase → Lipid degradation

Physiology-01.question: ৩) Site of blood cell production at late fetal life
Physiology-01.exp:
During late fetal life, the main site of blood cell production (hematopoiesis) is the red bone marrow.

Stages of fetal hematopoiesis:

  • Yolk sac → Early embryonic life (first site)

  • Liver → Major site during mid-fetal life

  • Red bone marrow → Becomes the major site in late fetal life and after birth 

Exam pearl
Hematopoiesis sequence:
Yolk sac → Liver → Spleen → Red bone marrow

  • Adult hematopoiesis: Red bone marrow (especially axial skeleton)

Physiology-01.question: ৪) Sky rise of ESR is found in
Physiology-01.exp:
A sky-high rise of ESR is classically seen in multiple myeloma.

Mechanism:

  • Multiple myeloma causes excessive production of immunoglobulins by malignant plasma cells.

  • Increased plasma proteins promote rouleaux formation of RBCs.

  • Rouleaux formation makes RBCs settle faster → markedly increased ESR (often >100 mm/hr).

Exam pearl:

  • Highest ESR → Multiple myeloma

  • ESR increases in: chronic inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, pregnancy, malignancy

  • ESR decreases in: Polycythemia vera (increased RBC mass slows sedimentation)

Physiology-01.question: ৫) Protein sub unit of microfilament is called
Physiology-01.exp:
The protein subunit of microfilaments is Actin.

  • Microfilaments are one of the three major components of the cytoskeleton.

  • They are composed mainly of actin filaments (F-actin), which are formed by polymerization of G-actin monomers.

  • Functions:

    • Maintain cell shape

    • Cell movement

    • Muscle contraction

    • Cytokinesis during cell division

Exam pearl:

  • Microfilament → Actin

  • Microtubule → Tubulin

  • Intermediate filament → Keratin (main example)

Physiology-01.question: ৬) Amount of plasma in blood
Physiology-01.exp:
Plasma constitutes about 55% of total blood volume.

Composition of blood:

  • Plasma → ~55% (water, proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, waste products)

  • Formed elements → ~45% (RBCs, WBCs, platelets)

The 45% formed element portion is mainly due to red blood cells and is represented by hematocrit (PCV).

Exam pearl:

  • Plasma = 55% of blood

  • Cells + platelets = 45% of blood

  • Hematocrit = percentage of blood occupied by RBCs (~45%)

Physiology-01.question: ৭) Which acts as microtubule-organizing centre?
Physiology-01.exp:
The centrosome acts as the microtubule-organizing centre (MTOC) of the cell.

  • Centrosome contains a pair of centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material.

  • It organizes microtubule formation and plays an important role in:

    • Formation of the mitotic spindle during cell division

    • Maintenance of cell shape and intracellular transport

Exam pearl:

  • Microtubule → Centrosome (MTOC)

  • Microfilament → Actin

  • Intermediate filament → Keratin

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis

Physiology-01.question: ৮) Mononuclear leukocyte
Physiology-01.exp:
Lymphocyte is a mononuclear leukocyte because it contains a single, round, non-segmented nucleus.

Classification of leukocytes:

  • Mononuclear leukocytes:

    • Lymphocytes 

    • Monocytes

  • Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (granulocytes):

    • Neutrophils

    • Eosinophils

    • Basophils

Exam pearl:
Mononuclear = Lymphocyte + Monocyte
Polymorphonuclear = Neutrophil + Eosinophil + Basophil (NEB)

Physiology-01.question: ৯) Most prevalent plasma protein
Physiology-01.exp:
Albumin is the most abundant (prevalent) plasma protein, making up about 60% of total plasma proteins.

Functions of albumin:

  • Maintains plasma oncotic pressure (major role)

  • Transports substances such as hormones, fatty acids, bilirubin, and drugs

Other plasma proteins:

  • Globulins → Immunity (antibodies), transport proteins

  • Fibrinogen → Blood clotting

  • Prothrombin → Coagulation factor (Factor II)

Exam pearl:

  • Most abundant plasma protein → Albumin

  • Major contributor to plasma oncotic pressure → Albumin

  • Clotting protein → Fibrinogen

Physiology-01.question: ১০) What is the way of message transmission in paracrine & autocrine communication?
Physiology-01.exp:
Paracrine and autocrine communication occur through the diffusion of chemical messengers in the interstitial fluid.

  • Paracrine signaling → A cell releases a chemical messenger that acts on nearby cells through local diffusion.

  • Autocrine signaling → A cell releases a messenger that acts on the same cell that secreted it.

Other communication types:

  • Directly from cell to cell → Gap junction/contact-dependent signaling 

  • Across synaptic cleft → Neural (synaptic) communication 

  • By circulating body fluids → Endocrine communication via blood 

Exam pearl:

  • Autocrine + Paracrine → Interstitial fluid diffusion

  • Endocrine → Blood circulation

  • Synaptic → Synaptic cleft

Physiology-01.question: ১১) Site of synthesis of albumin
Physiology-01.exp:
Albumin is synthesized in the liver by hepatocytes.

Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and its major functions are:

  • Maintaining plasma oncotic pressure

  • Transporting substances like:

    • Fatty acids

    • Bilirubin

    • Hormones

    • Drugs

Other options:

  • Spleen → Immune functions and removal of old RBCs, not albumin synthesis 

  • Plasma cells → Produce immunoglobulins (antibodies) 

  • Bone marrow → Produces blood cells, not plasma proteins 

Exam pearl:

  • Albumin → Liver

  • Immunoglobulin → Plasma cells

  • Fibrinogen & clotting factors → Liver

Physiology-01.question: ১২) Cell membrane is semipermeable because of having
Physiology-01.exp:
The cell membrane is semipermeable (selectively permeable) mainly because of its lipid bilayer structure.

  • The phospholipid bilayer has a hydrophobic core that allows only certain small, non-polar molecules to pass easily while restricting many ions and polar molecules.

  • Membrane proteins help in selective transport, but the basic semipermeability is mainly due to lipids.

Other options:

  • Protein → Helps transport substances (channels, carriers), but not the primary reason for semipermeability 

  • Carbohydrate → Mainly involved in cell recognition and receptors 

  • Glycolipid → Involved in cell recognition and membrane stability 

Exam parl:
Selective permeability of cell membrane → Phospholipid bilayer
Transport across membrane → Membrane proteins (channels/carriers)

Physiology-01.question: ১৩) Incorrect about serum
Physiology-01.option2: Contain some degradation products of clotting factors
Physiology-01.option4: Can be obtained from clot retraction
Physiology-01.exp:
Serum does not contain fibrinogen because fibrinogen is consumed during the clotting process to form fibrin. Therefore, serum is essentially plasma without clotting factors.

  • Serum = Plasma − Fibrinogen (and most clotting factors)

Other options:

  • High level of serotonin → Correct; serotonin is released from platelets during clotting and is present in serum 

  • Contains some degradation products of clotting factors → Correct; clotting process produces degradation products 

  • Can be obtained from clot retraction → Correct; serum is obtained after blood clot formation and retraction 

Exam pearl:
Plasma = Blood fluid + clotting factors (including fibrinogen)
Serum = Plasma − fibrinogen/clotting factors

Physiology-01.question: ১৪) Which organelle is important in specialized cellular signalling?
Physiology-01.exp:
The Golgi apparatus is important in specialized cellular signaling because it modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles that are delivered to specific cellular locations.

Functions of Golgi apparatus:

  • Protein modification (e.g., glycosylation)

  • Sorting and packaging of secretory proteins

  • Formation of secretory vesicles involved in cell communication/signaling

Other options:

  • Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) → Protein and lipid synthesis, especially rough ER for protein production 

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis (translation) 

  • Mitochondria → ATP production and apoptosis regulation 

Exam pearl:
Golgi apparatus = modification + packaging + sorting of proteins for secretion and signaling
Ribosome = protein synthesis
Mitochondria = energy production

Physiology-01.question: ১৫) Plasma protein is increased in
Physiology-01.exp:
Plasma proteins are increased in leprosy due to chronic infection causing increased production of immunoglobulins (globulins) as part of the immune response.

Causes of increased plasma proteins:

  • Chronic infections (e.g., leprosy, chronic inflammation) → ↑ globulins 

  • Multiple myeloma → ↑ immunoglobulins

Other options:

  • Malaria → May cause changes in plasma proteins but not a classic cause of increased total plasma protein 

  • Nephrotic syndrome → Causes loss of plasma proteins (especially albumin) in urine → hypoproteinemia 

  • Prematurity → Lower plasma protein levels due to immature liver function 

Exam pearl:

  • ↑ Plasma protein → Chronic infection, inflammation, multiple myeloma

  • ↓ Plasma protein → Nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, malnutrition, prematurity

Physiology-01.question: ১৬) Which is the force generator for muscle cell contraction?
Physiology-01.exp:
Myosin is the force generator for muscle cell contraction.

  • Myosin is a motor protein present in thick filaments of skeletal muscle.

  • Its heads bind to actin and perform a power stroke using energy from ATP, pulling actin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere → muscle contraction.

Other options:

  • Actin → Thin filament; provides the track on which myosin moves, but does not generate force itself 

  • Kinesins → Motor proteins involved mainly in microtubule-based intracellular transport 

  • Dyneins → Motor proteins for microtubule movement, cilia/flagella function and transport 

Exam pearl:

  • Force generator of muscle contraction → Myosin

  • Thin filament → Actin

  • Sliding filament mechanism → Myosin pulls actin using ATP

Physiology-01.question: ১৭) Lifespan of RBC in months
Physiology-01.exp:
The normal lifespan of a red blood cell (RBC) is approximately 120 days, which is about 4 months.

  • RBCs are produced in the red bone marrow.

  • Old and damaged RBCs are removed mainly by the spleen (also liver and bone marrow macrophages).

  • Hemoglobin is broken down into:

    • Globin → amino acids

    • Heme → iron + bilirubin

Exam pearl:

  • RBC lifespan → 120 days ≈ 4 months

  • Site of RBC destruction → Spleen (“graveyard of RBCs”)

  • Site of RBC production → Red bone marrow

Physiology-01.question: ১৮) Membrane transport system with downhill electrochemical gradient
Physiology-01.exp:
Facilitated diffusion is a membrane transport mechanism in which substances move down their electrochemical gradient through specific carrier proteins or channel proteins without using energy (ATP).

Features:

  • Movement: High concentration → Low concentration 

  • Requires membrane proteins (channels/carriers)

  • No ATP consumption

Other options:

  • Primary active transport → Moves substances against electrochemical gradient using ATP (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ pump) 

  • Co-transport (symport) → Secondary active transport; one substance moves downhill to drive another substance uphill 

  • Counter-transport (antiport) → Secondary active transport; exchange of substances in opposite directions 

Exam pearl:

  • Downhill transport without energy → Facilitated diffusion

  • Uphill transport using ATP → Primary active transport

  • Secondary active transport → Co-transport & Counter-transport

Physiology-01.question: ১৯) Erythropoietin is secreted from
Physiology-01.exp:
.

Erythropoietin (EPO) is mainly secreted by the kidney (peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex and outer medulla).

  • EPO secretion increases when there is hypoxia (low oxygen availability).

  • It stimulates the red bone marrow to increase RBC production (erythropoiesis).

Other options:

  • Liver → Produces EPO mainly during fetal life, but not the major adult source 

  • Lung → Gas exchange organ, not EPO secretion 

  • Bone marrow → Site of RBC production, not EPO secretion 

Exam pearl:

  • Adult EPO source → Kidney

  • Fetal EPO source → Liver (major)

  • EPO action → ↑ RBC production in bone marrow

Physiology-01.question: ২০) What is the site of Ca2+ storage and release for excitation-contraction coupling?
Physiology-01.exp:
The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is the site of Ca²⁺ storage and release during excitation–contraction coupling in muscle cells.

Mechanism:

  • Action potential travels along the sarcolemma and T tubules.

  • This stimulates the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release stored Ca²⁺.

  • Ca²⁺ binds with troponin C, causing movement of tropomyosin and allowing actin–myosin interaction → muscle contraction.

Other options:

  • Thick filament → Contains myosin; generates force 

  • Thin filament → Contains actin, troponin, tropomyosin 

  • T tubule → Conducts action potential deep into muscle fiber; does not store Ca²⁺ 

Exam pearl:

  • Ca²⁺ storage & release → Sarcoplasmic reticulum

  • Action potential conduction → T tubule

  • Force generation → Myosin (thick filament)

Physiology-01.question: ২১) Integral protein of RBC membrane
Physiology-01.exp:
Glycophorin is an integral membrane protein of the RBC (red blood cell) membrane.

RBC membrane proteins:

  • Integral proteins:

    • Glycophorin 

    • Band 3 protein (anion exchange protein)

  • Peripheral cytoskeletal proteins:

    • Spectrin

    • Ankyrin

Glycophorin contains carbohydrate chains that contribute to:

  • RBC surface charge

  • Cell recognition

  • Blood group antigen expression

Other options:

  • Ankyrin → Peripheral membrane protein connecting spectrin to Band 3 

  • Spectrin → Peripheral cytoskeletal protein maintaining RBC shape and flexibility 

  • Tropomyosin → Actin-associated muscle protein, not RBC membrane protein 

Exam pearl:

  • Integral RBC membrane protein → Glycophorin & Band 3

  • RBC cytoskeleton → Spectrin + Ankyrin

Physiology-01.question: ২২) Which of the following transport processes is involved if transport of glucose from the intestinal lumen into a small intestinal cell is inhibited by abolishing the usual Na+ gradient across the cell membrane?
Physiology-01.exp:
The transport of glucose from intestinal lumen into small intestinal cells occurs by Na⁺-glucose cotransport (SGLT-1).

  • It is a form of secondary active transport.

  • Glucose moves against its concentration gradient by using the energy stored in the Na⁺ electrochemical gradient.

  • The Na⁺ gradient is maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump on the basolateral membrane.

If the Na⁺ gradient is abolished, glucose transport stops → indicating Na⁺-dependent cotransport.

Other options:

  • Facilitated diffusion → Glucose moves through GLUT transporters down its gradient; does not depend on Na⁺ 

  • Primary active transport → Directly uses ATP (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ pump) 

  • Countertransport → Two substances move in opposite directions (antiport) 

Exam pearl:

  • Intestinal glucose absorption → Na⁺-glucose cotransport (SGLT-1)

  • Secondary active transport = Uses ion gradient, not direct ATP

  • Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase maintains Na⁺ gradient

Physiology-01.question: ২৩) Haeme containing proteins excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
Heme-containing proteins are proteins that contain a heme prosthetic group (iron-containing porphyrin ring).

Examples:

  • Hemoglobin → Contains heme; transports oxygen in RBCs 

  • Myoglobin → Contains heme; stores oxygen in muscle 

  • Cytochrome C → Contains heme; involved in mitochondrial electron transport chain 

cAMP (cyclic AMP) is not a heme-containing protein. It is a second messenger molecule derived from ATP and involved in intracellular signaling.

Exam pearl:

  • Heme proteins → Hemoglobin, Myoglobin, Cytochromes

  • cAMP → Second messenger (signal transduction), not a protein

Physiology-01.question: ২৪) Non protein nitrogenous substance in plasma excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
Non-protein nitrogenous (NPN) substances are nitrogen-containing compounds in plasma that are not proteins.

Examples of NPN substances:

  • Urea (major NPN component)

  • Uric acid

  • Creatinine 

  • Creatine 

  • Ammonia 

  • Amino acids

Protamine is a protein (a basic, arginine-rich protein), so it is not a non-protein nitrogenous substance.

Other options:

  • Ammonia → NPN substance 

  • Creatine → NPN substance

  • Creatinine → NPN substance 

Exam pearl:
NPN = Urea + Uric acid + Creatinine + Creatine + Ammonia
Protamine → Protein, not NPN

Physiology-01.question: ২৫) Normal Hb
Physiology-01.exp:
This question is slightly ambiguous because the major normal adult hemoglobin is Hb A (α₂β₂), which is not listed.

Among the given options, Hb F (Fetal hemoglobin, α₂γ₂) is a normal physiological hemoglobin found mainly during fetal life and present in small amounts in adults. ✅

Other options:

  • Hb C → Abnormal variant hemoglobin causing hemoglobin C disease

  • Hb S → Abnormal variant causing sickle cell disease 

  • Hb H → Abnormal β₄ tetramer seen in Hb H disease (α-thalassemia) 

Exam pearl:

  • Normal adult Hb → Hb A (α₂β₂)

  • Normal fetal Hb → Hb F (α₂γ₂)

  • Hb S → Sickle cell disease

  • Hb C → Hemoglobin C disease

  • Hb H → α-thalassemia (β₄ tetramer)

Physiology-01.question: ২৬) Non-Lethal value of body pH
Physiology-01.exp:
The normal blood pH is approximately 7.35–7.45. The body can tolerate only a narrow range of pH changes.

  • Lethal pH range: approximately <6.8 or >7.8 (severe acidosis or alkalosis can be fatal).

  • Therefore, among the given options, pH 7.0 is considered a non-lethal value.

Other options:

  • 6.5 → Severe acidosis; incompatible with life 

  • 6.8 → Near the lower lethal limit 

  • 8.2 → Severe alkalosis; lethal 

Exam pearl:

  • Normal blood pH → 7.35–7.45

  • Minimum survivable pH ≈ 6.8

  • Maximum survivable pH ≈ 7.8

Physiology-01.question: ২৭) What is true about nucleus of platelet
Physiology-01.exp:
Platelets (thrombocytes) are anucleate cell fragments, meaning they do not contain a nucleus.

  • They are derived from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.

  • Although they lack a nucleus, platelets contain:

    • Mitochondria

    • Granules (α-granules and dense granules)

    • Cytoskeletal proteins

Other options:

  • Single nucleus → Seen in many mononuclear cells (e.g., lymphocytes) 

  • Multiple nucleus → Seen in some giant cells, not platelets

  • Eccentric nucleus → Seen in plasma cells, not platelets 

Exam pearl:
Platelet = No nucleus + cytoplasmic fragment of megakaryocyte
RBC = No nucleus
WBC = Nucleated cells

Physiology-01.question: ২৮) Lysosomes contain -
Physiology-01.exp:
Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that are responsible for intracellular digestion and breakdown of various cellular components.

Lysosomal enzymes include:

  • Proteases → proteins

  • Lipases → lipids

  • Nucleases → nucleic acids

  • Glycosidases → carbohydrates

These enzymes work best in an acidic environment (pH ~5) maintained by proton pumps inside lysosomes.

Other options:

  • Hydrophobic enzymes → Not a classification of lysosomal enzymes 

  • Pro enzymes (zymogens) → Inactive enzyme precursors, mainly found in digestive secretions 

  • Growth hormones → Endocrine hormones, not lysosomal contents 

Exam pearl:
Lysosome = “suicide bag” of the cell → contains acid hydrolases (hydrolytic enzymes).

Physiology-01.question: ২৯) Primary clotting factor excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
Primary clotting factors are the major plasma coagulation proteins involved in the intrinsic and common pathways of coagulation.

  • Fibrinogen (Factor I) → Converted to fibrin during clot formation 

  • Prothrombin (Factor II) → Converted to thrombin; essential for coagulation 

  • Labile factor (Factor V) → A clotting factor of the common pathway 

  • Tissue factor (Factor III) → A cell membrane protein (thromboplastin) that initiates the extrinsic pathway, not a plasma clotting factor 

Exam pearl:

  • Factor I → Fibrinogen

  • Factor II → Prothrombin

  • Factor III → Tissue factor (not a plasma clotting factor)

  • Factor V → Labile factor

  • Extrinsic pathway starts with Tissue factor + Factor VII

Physiology-01.question: ৩০) The extrinsic pathway is assessed by...
Physiology-01.exp:
The extrinsic pathway of coagulation is assessed by Prothrombin Time (PT).

  • PT measures:

    • Extrinsic pathway → Factor VII

    • Common pathway → Factors X, V, II, I

Clinical importance:

  • Used to monitor warfarin therapy (vitamin K antagonist), because warfarin affects vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).

Other options:

  • BT (Bleeding Time) → Assesses platelet function and primary hemostasis 

  • CT (Clotting Time) → General coagulation test, less specific

  • APTT → Assesses intrinsic pathway (Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII) + common pathway 

Exam pearl:

  • PT → Extrinsic pathway → Factor VII → Warfarin monitoring

  • APTT → Intrinsic pathway → Heparin monitoringBT → Platelet function

Physiology-01.question: ৩১) Key reaction of coagulation in both pathway is
Physiology-01.exp:
The key reaction common to both intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways is the activation of Factor X (Xa).

  • Intrinsic pathway → Factors XII → XI → IX + VIII → Factor X activation

  • Extrinsic pathway → Tissue factor (III) + Factor VII → Factor X activation

  • Activated Factor X (Xa) with Factor V converts Prothrombin (Factor II) → Thrombin (Factor IIa), which converts fibrinogen into fibrin.

Other options:

  • Activation of Factor VII → Occurs in the extrinsic pathway only 

  • Activation of Factor II (Prothrombin) → Occurs after convergence at Factor X, not the common initiating step 

  • Activation of Factor XII → Intrinsic pathway only 

Exam pearl:
Intrinsic + Extrinsic pathways meet at → Factor X activation
Factor Xa + Factor V → Prothrombin → Thrombin → Fibrin clo

Physiology-01.question: ৩২) Synonym of clotting factor IX
Physiology-01.exp:
Clotting factor IX is also known as Antihemophilic B factor (Christmas factor).

  • Deficiency of Factor IX causes Hemophilia B (Christmas disease).

  • It is a component of the intrinsic pathway of coagulation.

Other options:

  • Antihemophilic A → Factor VIII deficiency → Hemophilia A 

  • Antihemophilic C → Factor XI deficiency 

  • Hageman factor → Factor XII 

Exam pearl:

  • Factor VIII → Antihemophilic A → Hemophilia A

  • Factor IX → Antihemophilic B (Christmas factor) → Hemophilia B

  • Factor XI → Antihemophilic C

  • Factor XII → Hageman factor

Physiology-01.question: ৩৩) Which enzyme is required in fibrinolysis?
Physiology-01.exp:
Plasminogen is the inactive precursor of the enzyme plasmin, which is the key enzyme responsible for fibrinolysis (breakdown of fibrin clot).

Mechanism:

  • Plasminogen → Plasmin (activated by tissue plasminogen activator, tPA)

  • Plasmin breaks down fibrin into fibrin degradation products (FDPs).

Other options:

  • Caspases → Enzymes involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death), not fibrinolysis 

  • Thrombin → Promotes clot formation by converting fibrinogen → fibrin 

  • Antithrombin III → Inhibits thrombin and other clotting factors; anticoagulant role 

Exam pearl:

  • Fibrinolysis → Plasmin (from plasminogen)

  • Clot formation → Thrombin → Fibrin

  • Clot breakdown → Plasmin → FDPs

Physiology-01.question: ৩৪) Intrinsic coagulation pathway starts with
Physiology-01.exp:
The intrinsic coagulation pathway starts with activation of Factor XII (Hageman factor).

Sequence of intrinsic pathway:

  • Factor XII → Factor XI → Factor IX → Factor VIII → Factor X

  • It is activated by contact with negatively charged surfaces (e.g., exposed collagen).

Other options:

  • Activation of Factor VII → Starts the extrinsic pathway 

  • Activation of Factor II (Prothrombin) → Occurs later when thrombin is formed 

  • Activation of Factor X → Common pathway step where intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge 

Exam pearl:

  • Intrinsic pathway → Factor XII (Hageman factor)

  • Extrinsic pathway → Factor VII + Tissue factor (III)

  • Common pathway → Factor X → II → I (Fibrinogen → Fibrin)

Physiology-01.question: ৩৫) Spontaneous arrest of bleeding is called
Physiology-01.exp:
Hemostasis is the process by which the body causes spontaneous arrest of bleeding after blood vessel injury.

Stages of hemostasis:

  1. Vasoconstriction → reduces blood flow

  2. Primary hemostasis → platelet plug formation

  3. Secondary hemostasis → coagulation and fibrin clot formation

  4. Clot stabilization and repair

Other options:

  • Homeostasis → Maintenance of internal body stability (temperature, pH, fluids, etc.), not specifically bleeding control 

  • Clot retraction → Shrinkage of formed clot due to platelet contraction; a part of hemostasis 

  • Fibrinolysis → Breakdown of fibrin clot after healing 

Exam pearl:
Arrest of bleeding → Hemostasis
Maintenance of internal environment → Homeostasis
Clot breakdown → Fibrinolysis

Physiology-01.question: ৩৬) Prothrombin time is
Physiology-01.exp:
Prothrombin Time (PT) is the time required for clot formation through the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

  • Normal PT ≈ 11–13 seconds (commonly taken as about 12 seconds).

  • It evaluates:

    • Extrinsic pathway → Factor VII

    • Common pathway → Factors X, V, II, I

Clinical use:

  • Monitoring warfarin (oral anticoagulant) therapy.

Other options:

  • About 30 sec → More consistent with APTT range, not PT 

  • About 18 sec → Not the normal PT value 

  • About 1 min → Too prolonged; abnormal 

Exam pearl:

  • PT → Extrinsic pathway → Factor VII → Warfarin monitoring → Normal ~12 sec

  • APTT → Intrinsic pathway → Normal ~30–40 sec

Physiology-01.question: ৩৭) A thrombus is composed of following except
Physiology-01.exp:
A thrombus is an abnormal blood clot formed inside a blood vessel during life. It is mainly composed of:

  • Fibrin → Forms the meshwork of the cloT

  • Platelets → Major component of arterial thrombi 

  • Red cells → Present especially in venous thrombi (red thrombus) 

White cells (WBCs) are not considered a major component of thrombus formation. 

Other options:

  • Fibrin → Essential structural component of thrombus 

  • Platelet → Forms platelet plug and contributes to thrombus 

  • Red cells → Trapped within fibrin network, especially in venous thrombosis 

Exam pearl:
Thrombus = Platelets + Fibrin + trapped blood cells (mainly RBCs)
Arterial thrombus → Platelet-rich (“white thrombus”)
Venous thrombus → RBC-rich (“red thrombus”

Physiology-01.question: ৩৮) INR in a healthy person -
Physiology-01.exp:
INR (International Normalized Ratio) is a standardized measure of Prothrombin Time (PT) used to assess the extrinsic coagulation pathway.

  • Normal INR in a healthy person is approximately 0.8–1.2 (commonly accepted range 0.9–1.3). 

  • Patients taking warfarin usually require a therapeutic INR of 2.0–3.0 (depending on indication).

Other options:

  • 1.5–1.8 → Mildly prolonged; not normal 

  • 4.0–5.0 → Excessively anticoagulated; increased bleeding risk 

  • 2.0–3.0 → Therapeutic range for many warfarin patients, not healthy individuals 

Exam pearl:

  • Normal INR → ~1

  • Warfarin therapy → INR usually 2–3

  • INR ↑ → Prolonged PT → Increased bleeding tendency

Physiology-01.question: ৩৯) Agglutinins are present in
Physiology-01.exp:
Agglutinins are antibodies present in the serum (plasma) that cause agglutination (clumping) of RBCs carrying corresponding antigens.

Example:

  • ABO blood group system:

    • Group A blood → Has anti-B agglutinin in serum

    • Group B blood → Has anti-A agglutinin in serum

    • Group O blood → Has both anti-A and anti-B agglutinins

    • Group AB blood → Has no ABO agglutinins

Other options:

  • RBC membrane → Contains agglutinogens (antigens), not agglutinins 

  • Platelet membrane → Contains platelet receptors, not agglutinins 

  • WBC membrane → Not the site of agglutinins 

Exam pearl:

  • Agglutinogens = Antigens on RBC membrane

  • Agglutinins = Antibodies in serum

  • Agglutination occurs when antibody reacts with corresponding RBC antigen

Physiology-01.question: ৪০) Which blood group has no antigen
Physiology-01.exp:
In the ABO blood group system, blood group O has no A or B antigens (agglutinogens) on the RBC membrane. 

  • Group A → Has A antigen on RBC surface and anti-B antibody in plasma 

  • Group B → Has B antigen on RBC surface and anti-A antibody in plasma 

  • Group AB → Has both A and B antigens on RBC surface and no anti-A/anti-B antibodies 

  • Group O → Has neither A nor B antigen on RBC surface; has anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma 

Exam pearl:

  • O group → No A/B antigen (universal RBC donor in ABO system)

  • AB group → No anti-A/anti-B antibody (universal plasma donor)

  • Agglutinogens = Antigens on RBC membrane

  • Agglutinins = Antibodies in plasma

Physiology-01.question: ৪১) Which can occur in excessive transfusion of blood with acid citrate dextrose
Physiology-01.exp:
In blood stored with acid citrate dextrose (ACD), citrate acts as an anticoagulant by binding ionized calcium (Ca²⁺). During massive or excessive blood transfusion, a large amount of citrate enters the circulation and temporarily reduces free calcium levels, causing hypocalcaemia.

Clinical features may include:

  • Muscle twitching

  • Tetany

  • Hypotension

  • Cardiac arrhythmia

Other options:

  • Hyperkalemia → Can occur with old stored blood due to leakage of potassium from RBCs, but not the main effect of ACD citrate 

  • Hypokalemia → Not a typical complication of ACD transfusion 

  • Hypercalcaemia → Citrate causes calcium reduction, not increase 

Exam pearl:
ACD blood transfusion → Citrate binds Ca²⁺ → Hypocalcaemia
Massive transfusion complications: Hypocalcaemia, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy

Physiology-01.question: ৪২) Properties of WBC except
Physiology-01.exp:
White blood cells (WBCs) have several important properties involved in body defense:

  • Phagocytosis → Engulfment and destruction of microorganisms by neutrophils and macrophages.

  • Diapedesis → Movement of WBCs through blood vessel walls into tissues.

  • Chemotaxis → Movement of WBCs toward chemical signals released from sites of infection or injury.

Pinocytosis means “cell drinking,” the uptake of extracellular fluid by cells. It is not considered a major property of WBCs in immune defense.

Other options:

  • Phagocytosis → Major function of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages 

  • Diapedesis → Essential for WBC migration into tissues 

  • Chemotaxis → Guides WBC movement to infection sites 

Exam pearl:
WBC properties → Amoeboid movement, Diapedesis, Chemotaxis, Phagocytosis
Pinocytosis → General cellular endocytosis, not a key WBC property

Physiology-01.question: ৪৩) Blood transfusion is essential in the following conditions except:
Physiology-01.exp:
Blood transfusion is indicated when there is a deficiency or loss of blood components.

  • Anemia → May require transfusion when severe or symptomatic due to low RBC/hemoglobin level.

  • Hemorrhage → Acute blood loss requires transfusion to restore blood volume and oxygen-carrying capacity.

  • Surgery → Blood transfusion may be needed during major surgeries with significant blood loss.

Polycythaemia is a condition with increased RBC mass and increased blood viscosity. Transfusion is not required; instead, treatment may involve phlebotomy (removal of blood).

Exam pearl:
Blood transfusion indications → Severe anemia, hemorrhage, major surgery
Polycythaemia → Excess RBCs → Treat by phlebotomy, not transfusion

Physiology-01.question: ৪৪) Stages of hemostasis excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
Hemostasis is the process that stops bleeding after vascular injury. The major stages of hemostasis are:

  1. Vasoconstriction → Reduces blood flow from the injured vessel.

  2. Platelet plug formation (Primary hemostasis) → Platelets adhere, activate, and aggregate.

  3. Coagulation of blood (Secondary hemostasis) → Formation of fibrin clot to stabilize the platelet plug.

Endothelial injury is the triggering event that initiates hemostasis, but it is not considered one of the stages of hemostasis.

Other options:

  • Vasoconstriction → First stage of hemostasis

  • Platelet plug formation → Primary hemostasis

  • Coagulation of blood → Secondary hemostasis

Exam pearl:
Stages of hemostasis = Vasoconstriction → Platelet plug formation → Coagulation
Endothelial injury = Initiating stimulus, not a stage

Physiology-01.question: ৪৫) Which play an important role in the defense mechanism of the body against the parasites?
Physiology-01.exp:
Eosinophils play an important role in the defense mechanism of the body against parasites, especially helminthic (worm) infections.

Functions of eosinophils:

  • Release major basic protein (MBP) and other toxic granules that damage parasites.

  • Involved in allergic reactions and modulation of inflammation.

  • Increased in parasitic infestations and allergic disorders.

Other options:

  • Neutrophil → Main defense against bacterial infections; phagocytosis of bacteria 

  • Basophil → Involved in allergy and histamine release 

  • Monocyte → Becomes macrophage; important in phagocytosis and chronic inflammation 

Exam pearl:
Eosinophils → Parasites + Allergy
Neutrophils → Bacteria + Acute inflammation
Basophils → Histamine + Allergy
Monocytes → Macrophages + Phagocytosis

Physiology-01.question: ৪৬) Which plays role in Phagocytosis?
Physiology-01.exp:
Neutrophils are the major cells involved in phagocytosis, especially during acute bacterial infections. They are the first leukocytes to reach the site of infection and engulf microorganisms.

Monocytes also perform phagocytosis after entering tissues and differentiating into macrophages. Since this is a single best answer MCQ, Neutrophil is the most appropriate choice.

Other options:

  • Basophil → Mainly involved in allergy and histamine release, not phagocytosis 

  • Eosinophils → Mainly defend against parasites and participate in allergic responses; limited phagocytic role 

  • Monocyte → Phagocytic cell, but less prominent as the first-line acute phagocyte compared with neutrophils 

Exam pearl:

  • Neutrophil → Most important phagocytic WBC in acute infection

  • Monocyte → Becomes macrophage; long-term phagocytosis

  • Eosinophil → Parasites

  • Basophil → Allergy (histamine)

Physiology-01.question: ৪৭) Cause of lymphocytopenia
Physiology-01.exp:
AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) causes lymphocytopenia, mainly due to destruction and reduction of CD4⁺ T lymphocytes by HIV infection.

  • HIV enters CD4⁺ T cells and causes progressive loss of these immune cells.

  • Reduced CD4 count leads to impaired cellular immunity and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

Other options:

  • TB → Usually causes immune activation and may show lymphocytosis, not a typical cause of lymphocytopenia 

  • Mumps → Viral infection that may cause lymphocytosis rather than lymphocytopenia 

  • Diphtheria → Bacterial infection; not a classic cause of lymphocytopenia 

Exam pearl:
Lymphocytopenia → HIV/AIDS, corticosteroids, radiation, immunodeficiency
AIDS hallmark → ↓ CD4⁺ T lymphocytes

Physiology-01.question: ৪৮) PCV increases in
Physiology-01.exp:
PCV (Packed Cell Volume) or Hematocrit increases when there is hemoconcentration (increased concentration of RBCs due to reduced plasma volume).

In Dengue shock syndrome, increased capillary permeability causes plasma leakage into tissues, leading to decreased plasma volume and increased PCV.

Other options:

  • Anemia → Decreased RBC mass → ↓ PCV 

  • Cirrhosis of liver → Often associated with anemia and fluid imbalance; not a typical cause of increased PCV 

  • Pregnancy → Plasma volume increases more than RBC mass → physiological hemodilution → ↓ PCV 

Exam pearl:
↑ PCV → Hemoconcentration (e.g., Dengue shock syndrome, dehydration, polycythemia)
↓ PCV → Anemia, pregnancy (physiological dilution)

Physiology-01.question: ৪৯) Factor decreasing ESR
Physiology-01.exp:
ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate) is the rate at which RBCs settle in plasma. Factors affecting ESR:

  • Increased specific gravity of RBCs → RBCs become heavier and settle more slowly → decreases ESR.

  • Increased blood viscosity → Slows RBC settling → decreases ESR.

  • Rouleaux formation → RBCs stack together, increasing sedimentation → increases ESR.

  • Increased size of RBCs (macrocytes) → Larger cells settle faster → increases ESR.

Other options:

  • Blood viscosity → Decreases ESR

  • Rouleaux formation → Increases ESR

  • Increased RBC size → Increases ESR

Exam pearl:
Factors decreasing ESR:

  • ↑ RBC specific gravity

  • ↑ Blood viscosity

  • ↓ Rouleaux formation

Factors increasing ESR:

  • Rouleaux formation

  • Anemia

  • Pregnancy

  • Inflammatory conditions (↑ fibrinogen)

Physiology-01.question: ৫০) Immature RBC is called
Physiology-01.exp:
A reticulocyte is an immature RBC (young red blood cell) that is released from the bone marrow into the bloodstream before becoming a mature erythrocyte.

  • Reticulocytes contain residual ribosomal RNA, which can be demonstrated by supravital staining.

  • They mature into fully functional RBCs within about 1–2 days in peripheral blood.

Other options:

  • Proerythroblast → Earliest nucleated precursor of RBC in bone marrow, not an immature circulating RBC 

  • Early normoblast → Nucleated erythroid precursor stage in bone marrow 

  • Intermediate normoblast → Developing erythroblast stage in bone marrow 

Exam pearl:
Immature RBC in blood → Reticulocyte
Normal reticulocyte count → ~0.5–2% of circulating RBCs
Reticulocyte count indicates bone marrow erythropoietic activity
